name: NQ-Open
summary: 3,610 real Google search questions, answered without a document to read, each with short reference answers from Wikipedia.
overview:
NQ-Open asks a system to answer a real search question with a short answer, without being given any document to read. Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, and Kristina Toutanova defined it in 2019 by taking the evidence away from Google's Natural Questions. They kept the questions that had a short answer, discarded the Wikipedia page each one had been annotated against, and dropped answers longer than five tokens, because "Answers with many tokens often resemble extractive snippets rather than canonical answers". Each example is only a question and its acceptable answers, and every question can be answered from English Wikipedia. [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.00300) and [NQ-Open README](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/natural-questions/blob/fb26a3073b1fe636c97302890a27b491d6530130/nq_open/README.md)

The questions are what set it apart. Natural Questions drew them from real anonymized, aggregated queries of eight words or more that several users had issued to Google search within a short period. Heuristics kept the queries that look like questions, and only those with a Wikipedia page among the top five search results went on to annotators, who marked a short answer on that page if it had one. The queries were collected in 2017 and 2018, and they read the way people type searches: lowercase, without question marks, and sometimes ungrammatical. [Natural Questions paper](https://aclanthology.org/Q19-1026/) and [EfficientQA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00133)

Because the Natural Questions test set is hidden, Lee et al. tested on its development set and held out part of the training set for development. Their retrieval model, ORQA, answered 33.3% of those 3,610 test questions exactly. The publisher's README lists later baselines on the same questions: REALM at 40%, DPR at 41%, and T5-XXL, which answers from its parameters alone, at 37%. NQ-Open was also the task of the NeurIPS 2020 EfficientQA competition, which used new development and test splits. [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.00300), [NQ-Open README](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/natural-questions/blob/fb26a3073b1fe636c97302890a27b491d6530130/nq_open/README.md), and [EfficientQA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00133)
methodology:
This snapshot contains the complete original NQ-Open development split: all 3,610 questions of `nq_open/NQ-open.dev.jsonl` at commit `fb26a30` of google-research-datasets/natural-questions. It is the split Lee et al. use as their test set, and the README notes that "almost all work to date has reported accuracy on the original NQ-open dev set". The 87,925-question training file and the EfficientQA development (1,800) and test (1,769) splits in the same folder are not imported; the README asks that any work using the EfficientQA test set say so explicitly. [NQ-Open README](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/natural-questions/blob/fb26a3073b1fe636c97302890a27b491d6530130/nq_open/README.md)

Each Task Prompt is the question exactly as published, in lowercase and without a question mark. No document comes with it, so a model must answer from what it knows or find evidence itself. The Solution lists the reference answers, one per line in the upstream order, and a prediction is correct when it matches any one of them. 2,076 questions have a single reference answer and 1,534 have between two and twenty-three, because the questions in this split were each annotated by five people and the references collect their short answers. [AmbigQA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.10645)

The source has no question IDs. Keys are `dev-0001` to `dev-3610`, from each question's line number in the pinned file, and prompt and solution links point to that line. Every question is distinct, which the official scorer relies on because it matches predictions to references by question text. The importer uses only Python's standard library. It reads the file at the pinned commit and checks the count, the fields, that questions are distinct, and that every question has non-empty answers of at most six words. It can be rerun with `python3 data/nq-open/import.py`.
scoring:
NQ-Open is scored as accuracy: the fraction of questions whose predicted answer matches a reference answer. The official script, `evaluate_predictions.py` from ORQA, normalizes the prediction and each reference by decomposing Unicode characters, lowercasing, removing punctuation and the articles a, an, and the, and collapsing whitespace. A prediction is correct when it equals any reference after that normalization. The EfficientQA organizers describe this as "exact match between predicted and reference answers after minor normalization", following Lee et al. [Evaluation script](https://github.com/google-research/language/blob/865fae65f63ef7e6b2989d4ff8b47f61750415a8/language/orqa/evaluation/evaluate_predictions.py), [normalization](https://github.com/google-research/language/blob/865fae65f63ef7e6b2989d4ff8b47f61750415a8/language/orqa/utils/eval_utils.py), and [EfficientQA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00133)

Exact match undercounts correct answers. In EfficientQA, human raters judged 13% of the predictions that matched no reference to be definitely correct and another 17% to be possibly correct. Under those ratings, most systems' accuracy rose by 17–25% and 41–54% respectively over the automatic score. The organizers note that five annotators' reference answers are often not exhaustive, so a correct answer phrased differently from every reference is scored wrong. [EfficientQA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00133)

Benchopedia's runner sends each question with an instruction to end the reply with a line `Answer: <answer>`. It takes the reply's last line, removes that label, and scores the rest with the official normalization and comparison. Each task is tried twice and passes a run only when both attempts pass.
limitations:
Many questions are ambiguous without the page they were annotated against. The AmbigQA authors annotated 14,042 NQ-Open questions and found that over half were ambiguous, with sources such as unclear event and entity references. NQ-Open keeps the answers to whichever reading its annotators chose, so a correct answer to another reading scores as wrong. [AmbigQA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.10645)

The answers are fixed to Wikipedia as it was in 2017 and 2018. Questions such as "when did the eagles win last super bowl" (reference: 2017) and "who won last year's ncaa women's basketball" (reference: South Carolina) depend on when they were asked, and a model that answers from more recent knowledge can be right and still score as wrong. [EfficientQA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00133)

The split is harder than NQ-Open's own training and development data, by construction. Its questions come from the Natural Questions development set, where five people annotated each question, and a question entered NQ-Open if any one of them found a short answer. Questions an annotator is unlikely to answer are therefore over-represented: 34.6% of the individual short-answer annotations in this split are null, and the majority of annotations are null for 33.9% of questions. Models score markedly lower on it than on NQ-Open's development split under the same conditions. [AmbigQA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.10645)

Much of the split can be answered by memorizing the training set. Lewis and colleagues found that 63.6% of the answers in this split also appear as answers in the NQ-Open training set, and that 32.5% of a sample of 1,000 questions have a near-duplicate paraphrase there, most differing by one or two words. Models scored far lower on the questions without such overlap. The questions and answers have been public since 2019 and the split carries no canary string, so a model may also have seen them in training. [Test-train overlap paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.02637)
